q1.question: A student places banana peels, dry leaves, and a small plastic wrapper into the same compost bin. What is the main problem with this mixture?
options: The plastic wrapper contaminates the composting process because it is not biodegradable
Dry leaves stop all microbial activity
Banana peels cannot decompose naturally
The mixture becomes hazardous B3 waste immediately
q1.explanation: Plastic contamination reduces compost quality because it does not biodegrade like organic material.

q2.question: In composting, why is moisture important but excessive water harmful?
options: Microbes need moisture, but excess water reduces oxygen and can create anaerobic conditions
Water prevents all decomposition
Excess water increases plastic recycling efficiency
Moisture turns organic waste into inorganic waste
q2.explanation: Composting requires a balance of moisture and oxygen. Too much water fills air spaces and limits aerobic decomposition.

q3.question: Look at the image of mixed food scraps and packaging. Which item should ELIO reject from the organic category?
options: Plastic food wrapper
Vegetable peel
Rice leftovers
Dry leaf
q3.explanation: A plastic wrapper is not organic waste and should be separated from compostable materials.

q4.question: Which condition most directly improves aerobic composting efficiency?
options: Balanced carbon-nitrogen ratio, sufficient oxygen, and suitable moisture
Keeping the pile fully sealed without air
Adding batteries to increase chemical reaction
Mixing compost with clean plastic bottles
q4.explanation: Efficient composting depends on carbon-nitrogen balance, oxygen availability, and moisture control.

q5.question: Why can meat or oily food waste be problematic in a simple classroom composting activity?
options: It may attract pests, produce odor, and slow controlled composting
It always becomes recyclable plastic
It cannot contain carbon
It makes composting completely impossible in every system
q5.explanation: Meat and oily foods can create odor and pest issues, especially in simple unmanaged composting systems.

q6.question: Based on the compost pile image, which observation indicates the pile may be too dry?
options: Materials look dusty, brittle, and decomposition appears slow
The pile has a balanced earthy smell
The pile is warm and slightly moist
Small decomposed particles are visible
q6.explanation: Very dry compost limits microbial activity and slows decomposition.

q7.question: ELIO detects a brown paper napkin with food residue. Why might it still be classified as organic/compostable in some contexts?
options: Because paper made from plant fibers can biodegrade if it is not coated with plastic or harmful chemicals
Because all paper is hazardous waste
Because food residue turns every object into metal
Because paper cannot ever be recycled or composted
q7.explanation: Uncoated plant-fiber paper with food residue can often be composted, depending on local rules.

q8.question: Which decision is best when ELIO detects an organic item covered with leaked battery fluid?
options: Classify it as contaminated hazardous waste instead of normal organic waste
Put it into compost because the base material is organic
Classify it as recyclable plastic
Ignore contamination because AI detection only uses shape
q8.explanation: Hazardous contamination changes the handling priority. Safety overrides the original material category.

q9.question: In the image, ELIO sees a wet leaf and a green plastic sachet. Which feature is most useful to distinguish them visually?
options: Natural irregular texture and vein pattern versus manufactured sealed edges
Both are green, so they must be the same category
Wetness alone proves both are organic
Size alone always determines the waste type
q9.explanation: Visual classification should consider texture, shape, edges, and material patterns, not color alone.

q10.question: Which explanation best connects organic waste management to environmental physics?
options: Decomposition involves energy transfer, temperature change, gas production, and material transformation
Organic waste management has no physical process
Only electrical circuits are part of environmental physics
Composting works by eliminating all matter from the system
q10.explanation: Composting can be connected to heat, gas exchange, matter transformation, and environmental systems.

q1.question: A plastic bottle still contains sugary liquid. Why should it not immediately be placed with clean recyclables?
options: Residue can contaminate other recyclables and reduce recycling quality
Liquid makes plastic become organic waste
Plastic bottles are always hazardous B3 waste
Sugar turns plastic into metal
q1.explanation: Food or liquid residue can contaminate recyclable materials and reduce processing efficiency.

q2.question: Which example best represents the 'Reduce' principle in 3R?
options: Using a refillable bottle instead of buying single-use plastic bottles
Throwing all bottles into one bin
Burning plastic waste to remove it quickly
Buying more packaged products because they are recyclable
q2.explanation: Reduce means preventing waste generation before it happens.

q3.question: Look at the image of plastic, metal, and food residue. Which item is most likely recyclable after cleaning?
options: Aluminum can
Banana peel
Used tissue with oil
Leaking battery
q3.explanation: Aluminum cans are commonly recyclable when separated and cleaned properly.

q4.question: Why is black plastic often harder for some automated sorting systems to detect?
options: Some optical systems may struggle because black plastic absorbs light and reduces sensor contrast
Black plastic is always organic
Black plastic always contains batteries
Color has no possible effect on visual detection
q4.explanation: In automated sorting, material color and reflectance can influence detection accuracy.

q5.question: Which factor is most important when deciding whether paper waste belongs in recycling or composting?
options: Whether it is clean/recyclable or contaminated with food and suitable for composting
Whether it is heavier than plastic
Whether it has any printed text
Whether it is placed near metal
q5.explanation: Clean paper can often be recycled, while food-contaminated uncoated paper may be composted depending on local rules.

q6.question: In the image, ELIO sees a transparent PET bottle and a glass bottle. Which feature helps distinguish them?
options: Shape details, surface reflection, thickness, and material appearance
Both are transparent, so they must be identical
Only color determines material
All transparent objects are hazardous
q6.explanation: Visual sorting should use multiple features such as shape, reflection, thickness, and material patterns.

q7.question: Why is source separation important for recyclable waste?
options: It reduces contamination and improves the quality of recovered materials
It makes every waste item biodegradable
It eliminates the need for any recycling facility
It changes hazardous waste into safe waste
q7.explanation: Separation at the source makes recycling more effective and reduces processing problems.

q8.question: Which item should not be treated as normal recyclable inorganic waste?
options: Broken compact fluorescent lamp
Clean plastic bottle
Empty aluminum can
Dry cardboard
q8.explanation: Compact fluorescent lamps can contain hazardous substances and require special handling.

q9.question: From the image, which sorting mistake would most reduce recycling quality?
options: Mixing oily food packaging with clean paper and plastic recyclables
Separating aluminum from plastic
Removing leftover liquid from a bottle
Flattening a clean cardboard box
q9.explanation: Oil and food residue can contaminate otherwise recyclable materials.

q10.question: Why is 'recyclable' not the same as 'automatically recycled'?
options: A material may be recyclable, but it still needs proper sorting, collection, cleaning, and processing
Recyclable materials disappear naturally
Recyclable means hazardous
Recyclable objects do not need human or system decisions
q10.explanation: Recycling depends on material condition, local facilities, sorting quality, and processing systems.

q1.question: Which property makes a waste item classified as hazardous B3?
options: It may be toxic, corrosive, flammable, reactive, or infectious
It is always green in color
It is always made of food material
It is always recyclable after washing
q1.explanation: Hazardous B3 waste is defined by danger properties such as toxicity, corrosivity, flammability, reactivity, or infection risk.

q2.question: A used battery is small and dry. Why should ELIO still separate it as hazardous?
options: It can contain chemicals and heavy metals that require special handling
Small objects are always organic
Dry objects cannot be hazardous
Batteries are safe if mixed with compost
q2.explanation: Batteries may contain harmful substances even when they look dry or small.

q3.question: Look at the image of mixed waste. Which item should be prioritized for hazardous separation?
options: Leaking battery
Clean paper
Banana peel
Empty plastic bottle
q3.explanation: A leaking battery poses chemical risk and should be handled separately as hazardous waste.

q4.question: Why should hazardous waste not be mixed with recyclable waste?
options: It can contaminate materials and create safety risks for handlers and recycling systems
It improves recycling quality
It makes plastic easier to compost
It removes all toxic properties
q4.explanation: Hazardous contamination can endanger people and damage recycling processes.

q5.question: A container has a faded warning label but no visible liquid. What is the safest classification decision?
options: Treat it as potentially hazardous until verified
Automatically classify it as organic
Mix it with clean paper
Ignore the label because it is faded
q5.explanation: When hazard information is uncertain, precaution is safer than mixing it with normal waste.

q6.question: In the image, which visual cue most strongly suggests hazardous handling is needed?
options: Warning symbol on the container
Round shape of the object
The object is placed on a table
The object is smaller than the others
q6.explanation: Hazard symbols communicate safety risks and should influence sorting decisions.

q7.question: Why is e-waste often treated differently from regular inorganic waste?
options: It may contain valuable recoverable materials and hazardous components
It is always compostable
It has no environmental impact
It can always be burned safely
q7.explanation: Electronic waste may contain both recyclable metals and hazardous substances, so it needs special management.

q8.question: What should ELIO prioritize if an object has both recyclable material and hazardous contamination?
options: Hazardous handling priority
Normal recyclable route
Organic composting route
Random sorting because categories overlap
q8.explanation: Safety comes first. Hazardous contamination should override ordinary recycling classification.

q9.question: From the image, which item should not be handled directly without protection?
options: Broken glass chemical container
Clean cardboard
Dry leaf
Empty water bottle
q9.explanation: A broken chemical container may cause both physical injury and chemical exposure.

q10.question: Which explanation best connects hazardous waste management with environmental physics?
options: It involves material properties, chemical energy, diffusion risk, containment, and exposure pathways
It only involves memorizing labels
It has no relation to physical systems
It only depends on object color
q10.explanation: Hazardous waste management connects to material behavior, transport, containment, energy, and environmental exposure.
